title: Emergence of Cumulative Witchcraft Concept
description: By around 1450, historians identify the coalescence of what Richard Kieckhefer called the 'cumulative concept of witchcraft' — the convergence of previously separate elements into a single criminal and theological category. These elements included traditional maleficium (harmful magic), the diabolical pact (theological concept from Augustine), the heretical sabbath (from inquisitorial prosecution of heretics), and night flight (from older folk traditions). Before this convergence, a person might be accused of harmful magic or of heresy separately; after it, the full composite crime combined all elements and presumed that any one element implied all others. This conceptual fusion, achieved roughly in the period 1420–1450 in Alpine inquisitorial practice, made the large-scale witch prosecutions of the following two centuries theoretically possible.
historiographical_note: Richard Kieckhefer's Magic in the Middle Ages (1989) and his earlier European Witch Trials (1976) are foundational for this periodization. Kieckhefer argued that the 'learned' elements of witchcraft (diabolism, sabbath) were imposed on traditional village magic beliefs through the inquisitorial process. Norman Cohn's Europe's Inner Demons (1975) offered a more radical version, arguing the entire diabolical framework was an elite fantasy with no folk basis.
source_method: Kieckhefer, Magic in the Middle Ages (1989); Cohn, Europe's Inner Demons (1975); secondary scholarship on the origins of the witchcraft concept
scholarly_disagreement: The precise dating and location of the cumulative concept's emergence is debated. Kieckhefer placed it in the Alpine regions c.1430-1450; others point to different regions or timeframes. Whether the synthesis was primarily elite-driven (Cohn) or involved genuine folk participation (Ginzburg, Wilby) remains contested.
